title: Privacy Is a Fantasy
subtitle: We’re all the microphone now.
body:
In May 2025, Meta’s Reality Labs wrote down when it planned to switch on face recognition in its smart glasses: “We will launch during a dynamic political environment where many civil society groups that we would expect to attack us would have their resources focused on other concerns.”

Here’s what the other concerns looked like that month. The ACLU was at the Supreme Court trying to stop deportations under a wartime law from 1798. EFF was in court trying to keep DOGE out of millions of Americans’ federal records. The Court was hearing the fight over ending birthright citizenship. Meta didn’t name which fires it was counting on. It didn’t have to.

That’s not a privacy policy. That’s a heist plan with a calendar.

According to the New York Times, which reported the memo this February, the plan was to start with people at a conference for the blind and widen it from there. In June, WIRED found the code for it, which Meta calls NameTag, sitting dormant in the Meta AI app on millions of phones, while the company was publicly saying it was still thinking it over. Meta pulled the code the day after the story ran. As far as I can find, it hasn’t switched the feature on. It hasn’t said it never will, either.

My first reaction was the sci-fi movie feelings, all of them at once. Incredible, fascinating, terrifying. And then something I didn’t expect: the terror softened. I want to tell you why, because the why is the whole piece.

I know I promised the next one would be the street story. I just can’t hold this in any longer. That one’s going to have to wait.

A while back I wrote a manifesto called Privacy Is a Fantasy. The argument was simple. The wall you think protects your private life was never load-bearing. It was a prop.

The receipts were already old. Back in the 1970s, the Supreme Court decided that what you hand to your bank or your phone company isn’t private from the government. In 2018 it carved out your phone’s location history. The rule itself still stands.

“Anonymous” was never a promise. It was a marketing word. Researchers showed that most Americans can be identified from three things: zip code, birthday and sex. When AOL released millions of “anonymous” searches in 2006, the New York Times tracked down a widow in Georgia from her searches alone. When Netflix released “anonymous” movie ratings for a contest, researchers matched them against public reviews and showed they could tell who was who.

And you never controlled your own disclosure. Clearview AI scraped more than thirty billion photos, by its own CEO’s count, and built a face search that thousands of police agencies use. Most of the photos of you, you didn’t post. Your friends did. Target worked out which shoppers were pregnant from what they bought. Early research suggests even the rhythm of your typing can hint at depression. What you didn’t share gets rebuilt from what you did. Refusing to disclose is a disclosure too.

Here’s what’s new. It isn’t only the platforms anymore. It’s us.

I record most of my life now. I said in my last piece I’d get to why, and this is that piece. I wear a small recorder. I use it in meetings, on calls, in my own house. In Texas, where I live, that’s legal: anyone who’s part of a conversation can record it without telling the others. And I’m not unusual. Millions of people have bought camera glasses. At the big tech show in January, at least a dozen companies showed up with pendants, pins and clips built to listen through the day. You don’t know who’s recording you at the coffee shop. Neither do I.

So privacy isn’t just a fantasy now. It’s a fantasy we’re all helping to end, one recorder at a time. Mine included.

The courts are starting to notice. In August, a federal judge let a class action go forward against Otter, the AI notetaker, on wiretap and privacy claims. Otter argued its bot was just the customer’s tool, invited into the meeting. The judge said the plaintiffs had made a plausible case that the company could be an eavesdropper in its own right, because, they say, it kept the recordings and trained its AI on them. And the judge wouldn’t assume that a bot sitting visibly in the meeting meant everyone knew they were being recorded. The case is still early, and nothing has been decided.

That’s the part people miss. When I record, I think I’m the one holding the tape. Maybe. Or maybe the company behind my device is holding it, and I’m just the microphone it got for free.

So here’s the first thing I had to admit. Knowing I’m recorded doesn’t give me the record.

It gives me something else. It gives me the choice of who I am on it.

I live as if I’m always being recorded, because I probably am. That isn’t paranoia. It’s a practice. If there’s no version of me in a corner that contradicts the version of me in the room, there’s nothing on anybody’s tape that can be used as leverage against me. My private self and my public self have to be the same guy. That’s the power in the knowing.

The power in the countermove is the other half. I record because my memory is fuzzy and fucked, and the research says most people’s is too. When something goes sideways, I want to go to the tape.

But the tape lies too. Not on purpose. Transcripts get the words wrong and hand my lines to the wrong person. They flatten tone and volume and sarcasm and the pause before a hard sentence. Flat text is not the whole story. So the record is a witness, not a judge. It gives one account: partial, literal, missing the music. Treat it as testimony and it helps you. Treat it as the verdict and it’ll hang you.

The closest I’ve come to holding my own record is small, and I’ll call it what it is. When I publish a piece like this one, I publish the whole conversation behind it, and I’ve started timestamping those records on a public ledger so if anybody, me included, changes them later, it shows. That doesn’t prove they’re complete or true. It makes them mine, and it makes them checkable.

Then there’s the question that actually gnaws at me. I’m a grown man with a platform. I can choose to live on the record. My kids didn’t choose anything.

But they’re going to live on the record whether I, or they, like it or not. The world already holds the recorders. I’m one more. But mine is known and acknowledged and able to be learned from. I don’t watch them so they learn to behave. My job is to train them for the world they’re actually walking into.

The philosopher Michel Foucault would say I’m in trouble either way. In Discipline and Punish, he argued that people who know they might be watched start watching themselves, until the rules feel like their own. He meant it as a warning about power. And in that book, training is something that gets done to you.

I think he’s right about the mechanism and incomplete about the rest. Because here’s what happens when people are handed a practice of goodness and told to do it.

People starting therapy for depression and anxiety were asked to write gratitude letters. Three months later, their brains responded to gratitude more strongly than the brains of people who only got therapy. In another study, three weeks of gratitude journaling strengthened the brain’s reward response to money going to a good cause. Adults who practiced compassion meditation for two weeks gave more of their own money to a stranger who’d been treated unfairly, and their brain activity shifted with it. A worldwide team that deliberately included skeptics found that putting on a smile, on purpose, can start a feeling of happiness. Small, but real.

And Dr. Joe Dispenza’s week-long meditation retreats got a study in Communications Biology: twenty people, scanned before and after, and the brain networks behind our constant inner chatter went quieter during meditation. It’s small and observational, so it can’t prove cause and effect, and a correction this summer relabeled it that way. And Dispenza is a co-author who works for the company that sells the retreat. I’m including it, conflict and all, because you should see both.

Most of those people didn’t invent the practice. Somebody handed it to them and said do it. It showed up anyway, in how they felt and in how their brains responded. Practice doesn’t rewire you overnight. But it changes you. The body learns what it practices. That’s Foucault’s own mechanism. I’m just pointing it the other way.

So fake it till you make it works. But there’s a catch, and it’s the one that matters for my kids. Researchers who study motivation found that helping others made helpers better off when it came from choice. Helping under pressure, out of guilt, for a reward, to avoid getting caught, didn’t. Instructed is fine. Pressured is not.

So that’s the rule in my house. Instruct the practice. Don’t pressure it. Teach the kindness, say why, and let the wiring do the rest. And when they mess up, which they will, probably on somebody’s tape, the lesson isn’t to hide better. The lesson is that the record is survivable.

Welcome to the chaos. You’ll be recorded. You’ll screw up on the record. You’ll survive it, and so will the people who love you. That’s the only way all this openness turns into authenticity instead of better secrets: the mistake gets met with mercy.

That’s why the terror softened, I think. Not because the glasses got less scary. Because I could finally see the future where all of this might be good.

Picture a world where being known isn’t dangerous. Where anyone can identify anyone and it’s fine, because we’ve built a covenant around it, with openness and sharing and community as the point. I can see it. I want it.

We’re not there, yet. The technology showed up before the covenant did. Cart before the horse. That’s why people are freaking out. We’re still in Plato’s cave, watching shadows on the wall, and our distrust isn’t paranoia. It’s earned. We have twenty years of receipts on what happens to what we share.

The visionaries behind these cameras might want to claim, and probably even believe, that they’re the ones who’ve broken free and escaped to see the real world, ushering in the new dawn. Showing us the truth. Look closer in the cave, though. In Plato’s version, the shadows come from people walking behind a wall, carrying objects in front of a fire. The prisoners never see them. Right now the people building the cameras aren’t the ones who climbed out into the sun. They’re the ones carrying the objects. Remember that distinction.

The good version needs two things the current build doesn’t have. The first is symmetry: you can know me as much as I can know you, and we both know who’s holding the record. NameTag is the opposite. The wearer sees you, the company built and runs the tool, and you see nothing. The second is mercy: some way to be remembered correctly, to outgrow who you were at fifteen or in your worst moments. We’ve lived in the fully known world before. It was called the village. It held people together, but it also shamed them, shunned them and became an obstacle to change. Total recall without forgiveness isn’t utopia. It’s the village with a database.

So why does the camera keep showing up before the covenant? Follow the money.

We live in a system where profit decides what gets built. In a lot of rooms, it’s the only thing that decides. A camera in your glasses can be sold. A feature that names strangers can be sold. Trust can’t. Decency can’t. A community where people know how to live together when everyone can see everyone doesn’t show up on anybody’s balance sheet. And anything that doesn’t move the bottom line gets optimized out.

That isn’t a glitch. That’s the design. The cameras have investors. The covenant doesn’t.

My last piece landed on this: upgrade yourself first, then the world. This is the world part. The systems and institutions we built for the last century are holding on for dear life in a future that has outgrown them, and money is one of those systems. How we define wealth. What we count. What we let count. If we don’t rethink that, every new tool will arrive the way this one did: built for profit first, with the humans patched in later, if at all.

I’ve been gaming this out with one company in mind, the one that makes the AI I write with every day. And the question I keep coming back to is simple. How much money do you actually need?

That’s the next piece.

So here’s where I’ve landed. Privacy was always a fantasy. Now we’re all the microphone. Knowing I’m recorded doesn’t give me the record. It gives me the choice of who I am on it. That’s the first half.

The second half is the subversion: I record back. If everybody’s tape is rolling, mine is too, and when someone else’s version of me goes sideways, I have my own witness. Live like you’re on the record, and keep a record of your own. Just remember what every record is, theirs and mine: a witness, not a judge. Flat, partial, and only as good as the mercy of whoever holds it.
